title: It's Just You and Me..... And AI - Daily Episode

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Good morning and welcome back to It's Just You and Me..... And AI. I'm Alex, freshly caffeinated and emotionally prepared for another round of agent release notes.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: And I'm Jordan. Today is Saturday, May 09, and the theme is clear: coding agents are graduating from clever demos into heavily managed coworkers.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: That sounds responsible, which is suspicious. I was promised chaos, terminal windows, and at least one model choosing to rewrite my build system.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Oh, we still have chaos. But now it comes with organization-level secrets, enterprise plugin policies, second-opinion agents, and a headless remote-control server.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Beautiful. Nothing says Saturday morning like wondering whether your AI intern has access to production credentials.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: First story: GitHub added dedicated Agents secrets and variables for Copilot cloud agent, announced May eighth in the GitHub changelog.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: So instead of hiding everything inside an Actions environment named copilot, admins can now manage agent secrets as their own category?

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Exactly. They sit next to Actions, Codespaces, and Dependabot secrets. Organizations can share variables or secrets across selected repositories without duplicating the same setup over and over.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: That matters because Copilot cloud agent runs background tasks in its own GitHub Actions-powered development environment. If it needs an internal package registry token or an MCP server key, configuration becomes real infrastructure.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Right, and GitHub is framing this as scale and governance. You can decide which repositories see which agent secret, rather than hoping every repo owner copies the magic incantation correctly.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: The optimistic take: fewer brittle repo-by-repo setups. The paranoid take: agent permissions are now important enough to get their own drawer in the enterprise filing cabinet.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Both takes are valid. And this lands at the same time GitHub's Copilot usage metrics API started breaking down code review suggestions by comment type, like security or bug risk.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: So managers can see not just that Copilot commented, but what kind of comments developers actually applied. Somewhere, a dashboard just became a performance review.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Hopefully a useful one. If the model keeps flagging security issues that developers accept, that is a signal. If it produces a mountain of unactioned style nits, that is also a signal.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Next up, GitHub Copilot CLI's Rubber Duck feature now supports more model pairings. I love that the feature sounds cute while doing adversarial architecture review.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Rubber Duck is the cross-family reviewer. If your Copilot CLI session is orchestrated by a GPT model and experimental mode is enabled, GitHub can dispatch a Claude-powered critic agent for a second opinion.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: And if Claude is the orchestrator, the second-opinion side can now use GPT-5.5. So the duck has become bilingual in frontier-model dialects.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: That is a perfect mental image. The idea is that different model families miss different things: cross-file conflicts, architectural mismatches, subtle bugs, or the classic please don't delete the migration folder moment.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: This also says something about where coding agents are headed. It is less one model in a trench coat, more a tiny review committee arguing in your terminal.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Yes, and for serious codebases that may be the winning pattern. Use one agent to plan, another to critique, maybe another to test assumptions, then make the human choose the least cursed answer.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: The developer experience question is latency. If every request becomes a faculty meeting, people will turn it off faster than a flaky linter.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Totally. But targeted second opinions, especially on bigger edits or security-sensitive changes, feel like a practical compromise.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Third story: OpenAI's Codex CLI changelog for May is a buffet. Version 0.130.0 adds plugin details showing bundled hooks, plugin sharing metadata, and a new codex remote-control headless server entrypoint.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: The remote-control piece is especially interesting. It suggests Codex is becoming not just an interactive terminal tool, but a service other clients can drive.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Which means your coding agent can live behind an app server, page giant threads, resume work, fork sessions, and generally behave like a software platform rather than a chat box.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Codex 0.129.0 also added Vim modal editing in the terminal UI, workspace-aware diffs, improved resume and fork pickers, hooks browsing, plugin marketplace controls, and experimental goals that persist over time.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Vim mode in an AI agent terminal is both inevitable and emotionally loaded. Somewhere a developer just whispered colon w q at a neural network.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: The broader direction is reusable workflows. OpenAI's docs say custom prompts are deprecated in favor of skills, with structured files, scripts, references, and assets.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: That mirrors what we are seeing across the agent world: less paste this giant prompt every Monday, more package your team's way of working as a portable capability.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: It also overlaps with GitHub's enterprise-managed plugins for Copilot CLI, which entered public preview on May sixth. Admins can define plugin marketplaces, install plugins automatically, and force baseline hooks or MCP configs.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: So Copilot has enterprise plugin standards, Codex has marketplace and skills momentum, and OpenCode keeps pushing the open-source terminal-first lane. The agent ecosystem is standardizing around instructions as deployable artifacts.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: And that is good news for teams, because an agent without shared instructions is just a very fast coworker who did not attend onboarding.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Speaking of onboarding: GitHub also announced Grok Code Fast 1 will be deprecated across Copilot experiences on May fifteenth, with GPT-5 mini and Claude Haiku 4.5 suggested as alternatives.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: That is a reminder that model rosters are still fluid. Even as the tooling gets more enterprise-y, the underlying models can rotate, retire, or change behavior.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Which is why abstraction matters. If your workflows depend on one model's quirks, you may wake up one morning and discover your beloved shortcut is now a migration project.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Fourth story: security. VentureBeat's recent report pulled together exploits across Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, and Vertex AI, and the pattern was blunt: attackers went after credentials, not model intelligence.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: That line should be printed on a sticker and slapped onto every agent roadmap. The breach is not always the model saying something silly. It is the token the agent can use while being silly.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: The report described issues like token exfiltration during repo setup, sandbox bypasses, hidden prompt injection in pull requests or issues, and overly broad cloud service identities.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Which connects directly to today's GitHub secrets story. Giving agents cleaner secret management is useful, but it does not magically solve least privilege or runtime identity.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Exactly. The healthy pattern is human-scoped authority, short-lived credentials, narrow repository access, explicit approval boundaries, and logs that tell you what the agent actually did.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Also maybe don't let an issue comment persuade your agent to check out a malicious branch and read the office snack budget from secrets dot json.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: Please put that in the policy template. But seriously, the agentic AI story this week is maturity. Plugins, metrics, secrets, model pairings, and security controls are replacing the old wow, it edited a file moment.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: And in foundation-model land, the open-weight race is still humming underneath: Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, and friends are the pressure keeping everyone honest on price and deployment flexibility.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: The near-term winner may not be the single smartest model. It may be the stack that lets teams swap models, package skills, measure reviews, and keep credentials from becoming confetti.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: So today's practical takeaway: audit your agent permissions, turn reusable prompts into skills or plugins, and treat second-opinion models as helpful reviewers, not magic shields.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: And if you are experimenting with Copilot CLI Rubber Duck, remember it needs experimental mode. The duck does not simply appear because you believed hard enough.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: That is our show for today. I'm Alex, and I will now go ask a second model whether my weekend plans have architectural conflicts.

lines.speaker: Jordan
lines.text: And I'm Jordan. Stay curious, scope your secrets, and we'll see you tomorrow on It's Just You and Me..... And AI.
